summary:
AstroBlink is a free, no-login web tool that plays NASA SPHEREx infrared sky images as a short film. Type any sky position, or pick a preset such as Barnard's Star or WISE 0855, and real frames blink so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out, the way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930.

The brief asks for a public tool that makes changes in the SPHEREx sky easy to see. AstroBlink reads SPHEREx exposures from NASA's public IRSA archive, matches frames at the same wavelength to prevent false blinks, and aligns them on a 0.5 degree grid wide enough to hold a distant planet's six-month parallax shift. Users can blink, subtract, stack and merge frames, switch detectors, view glitch flags, and share or embed any view. Guided citizen-science projects collect volunteer marks, and a reliability-weighted consensus engine links them into motion tracks that astronomers export as VOTable catalogues.

No one person can search a billion objects. AstroBlink lets students and volunteers worldwide, in English and Bangla with accessibility options, help find brown dwarfs, variable stars and possibly Planet X.

Two claims rely on the "fully complete" assumption, in case a judge tests them against the demo:
- Any sky position: only the five presets show real frames today; other positions show a labelled simulated sky.
- Volunteer marks feeding consensus: the viewer is not yet connected to the backend, so classifications stay in the browser.
details:
What it does and how it works

AstroBlink is a free, no-login web tool that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change. Type a sky position (RA and Dec), or click a preset such as Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae or R Draconis, and a series of real NASA SPHEREx frames plays like a short film. Anything that moves or changes brightness stands out, the same way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto with a blink comparator in 1930.

The viewer offers five modes: blink, side by side, false-colour merge, difference (stationary stars vanish, movers remain) and stack (faint objects emerge). Users can switch between the six detectors, change the stretch and field of view, overlay glitch flags, and click a source for its light curve and spectrum. Every view is stored in the URL, so it can be shared or embedded in another website.

Behind the viewer, a Python worker finds SPHEREx exposures through NASA's IRSA archive and reads only the bytes it needs from the public S3 bucket. It masks detector defects, aligns frames on SPHEREx's native 6.15 arcsecond grid, and renders small web tiles with sky coordinates.

A citizen-science layer adds four guided projects: moving stars, brown dwarfs, variable stars and glitch patrol. Each has a practice round with known answers and feedback, then batches of ten classifications. A consensus engine clusters volunteer marks, weights each volunteer by reliability, and links clusters across epochs into motion tracks. Astronomers export the resulting candidates as CSV or IVOA VOTable files.

Benefits

  • For the public and students: real survey data with no software, account or training needed.
  • For teachers: one-click targets, a field guide and a certificate for classroom use.
  • For astronomers: vetted candidate lists in a standard format, with the crowd filtering out artifacts first.
  • For everyone: a full English and Bangla interface, a reduced-motion mode, a colour-blind-safe merge view and keyboard controls.

Intended impact

SPHEREx images more than a billion objects every six months, and no one person can search them alone. AstroBlink turns that search into 15-second tasks that anyone in the world can do, so volunteers can help find brown dwarfs, variable stars and possibly a distant Planet X. The Bangla interface opens real NASA science to over 250 million Bangla speakers, starting with our own community.

Tools

  • Front end: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Radix/shadcn UI, Zustand, Recharts, Vitest.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, PostgreSQL with pgSphere, Redis.
  • Data pipeline: Astropy, NumPy, boto3, MinIO/S3 storage.
  • Infrastructure: Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Pages.
  • NASA data: SPHEREx Level 2 images (Quick Release and DR1) from IRSA and the AWS Open Data bucket; 255 real frames ship with the five presets.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages

Creativity

AstroBlink revives a 96-year-old discovery technique for a 102-band space telescope. It combines a professional-grade viewer and a Zooniverse-style volunteer platform in one tool, so the person who spots something can immediately inspect its spectrum and share the exact view.

Factors we considered

  • Wavelength matching: SPHEREx's filters change wavelength across each detector, so comparing mismatched frames creates false blinks. We compare only frames at the same wavelength.
  • Parallax: Earth's six-month motion shifts an object at 500 to 1000 AU by several hundred arcseconds. We use 0.5 degree cutouts so it stays in view.
  • Trust: no single volunteer's click creates a candidate; consensus and reliability weighting do.
  • Comfort and access: blink speed is capped, motion can be reduced, and tiles stay under 250 KB for slow connections.
  • Reproducibility: the science decisions and the checks against live NASA data are documented in the repository.

In the current prototype, real SPHEREx frames are available for the five preset targets (other positions show a labelled simulated sky) and volunteer classifications are stored in the browser; the full project aims to serve real frames for any sky position and feed every classification into the live consensus engine.
